# Conclusion

In July 2025, the UK government\'s 10 Year Health Plan for England[^c6-1] set out three shifts: from hospital to community, from treatment to prevention and from analogue to digital. The palliative care sector recognised itself in all three, and was right to. Hospices have been practicing community-based, holistic, anticipatory care for decades. The shifts essentially describe what the sector has always argued for.

There is a timely opportunity now, but it also captures the gap in the system. The shifts describe an end state that the palliative and end-of-life care system is not consistently, equitably delivering, and the reasons are structural rather than simply clinical. Late acute admissions at end of life remain common, not because the clinicians want them but because the alternative depends on out-of-hours cover, coordination and community capacity and readiness that exists in some pockets but not elsewhere. Care homes are on track to become the most common place of death, whilst staffed by workers who have little or no training to provide compassionate, timely palliative and end of life care. Care records cannot be written across the boundaries of hospices, primary care, acute and community trusts and hospice data is not linked to the NHS at all. None of this is a failure of intent, but a symptom of what happens when a system is funded to do one thing and asked to do another.

This report has mapped where the gaps can be closed. The emerging opportunities we have identified range widely in their leverage to impact the system. At one end sit interventions that change what information moves and how - shared care records, digital infrastructure, coordinated points of access - where the problem is well-defined and the intervention logic is close to linear. In the middle sits changes to how the system is organised. Care home staff trained and ready to provide palliative care, coordination hubs that hold the holistic picture of a family. At the furthest end sits opportunities to change what a society is capable of. Improving our awareness and understanding of death, dying and caregiving with practical and relational competencies to support people dying in their neighbourhood. These emerging opportunities have different orders of difficulty and complexity and different orders of return. An impactful platform needs some of each.

Above all, what has been missing is not the ideas, but the forms of capital capable of backing them. The structured philanthropic picture for this field is thin. Our analysis of a decade of open grants data has found over £9m a year going into palliative and end-of-life care, often in grants of a few thousand pounds, overwhelmingly directed to institutions rather than to infrastructure, innovation or systems change. Across ten years, 2 grants mention digital. There is no strategic systems-change funder in this field at all.

When the money does arrive, the instruments constrain it. 3-year cycles end before a new practice can be embedded and sustained, with the evidence that would justify further funding is unable to be produced within that timeframe, resulting in a double bind. We have found that restricted funding often lands on building-based models of care, which sustains the paradigm that the shifts are trying to move beyond. A deeper financial paradox lies in the fact that saving is real to the system, but not to any single budget line. Shifts are made to reduce admissions, but hospital and hospice beds are refilled.

This is an argument for philanthropy, which is narrow and specific. Philanthropic capital does not need to save the return. It can move across boundaries between public NHS, for-profit care homes and the charitable hospice sector. It can hold a position long enough for evidence to mature and connect with reliable adoption by meeting the needs of other parts of the system. It can fund something whose value is real but unreliable, and can do so without knowing the answer in advance. It can also plan its own exit. We believe the most durable philanthropic investments are designed from the start, with their own end in mind. They are designed to know who sustains it, with what evidence under what conditions. That approach is largely absent from this system, and its absence is one large reason why good work keeps falling off the cliff.

It is important to note we are not proposing to do this *to* the sector, but *with* it. The models that need to scale already exist in places, and are held by the teams who built them. What they often lack is capital, patient enough to prove them and coordinated enough to move beyond the original place that created them. Equally true, is that some of what is needed does not exist yet and will need to be seeded, and built. This reinforces the need for a collaborative approach rather than a single funder.

**Next steps for Phase 2**

Between September and November we will turn what has surfaced into propositions a donor collaborative could fund.

Working from the opportunity spaces in Chapter 4, we expect to narrow to five or six. Selection will weigh whether the opportunity sits in the 2nd horizon rather than sustaining "business as usual"; whether philanthropic capital is genuinely the right instrument and whether the work can travel beyond the place that produced it. Each proposition will set out its problem, theory of change, indicative cost, intervention type and measurement framework, developed alongside the causal loop map.

One challenge we bring into the next phase is that the evidence easiest to produce is short-order and clinical, while the highest-leverage work needs a different language of proof. A collaborative that funds only what is easiest to measure will fund the first horizon by default.

Beyond the immediate next phase, in the early winter we will convene sector leaders, practitioners, commissioners, funders and people who have cared for someone at the end of life, to stress-test the propositions before anything is committed. The revised thesis and map will then be published openly.
